fetched_contents.text: Controlled moisture permeability of thermoplastic starch/polylactic acid/poly butylene adipate-co-terephthalate film for the autolysis of straw mushroom Volvariella volvacea Highlights * • The moisture permeability of the film was adjusted by changing the TPS content. * • The autolysis of straw mushrooms decreased by adjusting moisture permeability. * • The TPS30/PLA/PBAT film inhibited the autolysis of straw mushrooms most strongly. Abstract Straw mushrooms are prone to autolyze, leading to a high requirement of environmental humidity. In this work, thermoplastic starch/polylactic acid/poly (butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (TPS/PLA/PBAT) film was produced by extrusion. The moisture permeability of the film was controlled by adjusting the content of TPS, which could be expected to further control humidity of the microenvironment in the package. Results revealed that the water vapor transmission rate of the film linearly increased from 612.31 g/m2·24 h to 1082.50 g/m2·24 h with the increase in the TPS concentration. The TPS/PLA/PBAT film with 30 wt% TPS showed the strongest inhibition on the autolysis of straw mushrooms compared with other groups, effectively delaying the increase in the free water, soluble solid content, rate of weight loss, and polyphenol oxidase of straw mushrooms and extending the shelf life of straw mushrooms from 24 h to 72 h. Keywords Starch ; Film ; Moisture permeability ; Straw mushroom ; Autolysis Introduction Straw mushroom (Volvariella volvacea) is widely grown in most parts of Asia, especially China. Its unique flavor, high nutritional value, and medicinal properties lead to its high demand (Fang et al., 2019). It is a highly perishable commodity because of its high moisture content (∼90%, wet basis). In addition, its high respiration rate, high microbial activity, and low textural strength limit the shelf life of this mushroom to 1–2 days after harvest (Dhalsamant, Dash, Bal, & Panda, 2015). Similar to other commercial mushrooms, V. volvacea may suffer from autolysis, water loss, browning, physical damage, and microbiotic invasion due to its high moisture content of fruiting body without the presence of cuticles, leading to its highly perishable characteristics during storage, transportation, and shelf life (Fang et al., 2019). Packaging is an effective way to control the microenvironment by reducing the rate of respiratory metabolism (Jiang et al., 2020). At present, the development of sustainable food production and biodegradable packaging materials with better functionality and processability are drawing extensive attention from researchers and industries because the application of biodegradable packaging materials is expected to reduce environmental problems (Srisa and Harnkarnsujarit, 2020). Biopolymers have gained significant attention in the packaging industries due to their biodegradability and abundant availability from various natural sources, making them effective alternatives for fossil-based plastics (Rangaraj, Rambabu, Banat, & Mittal, 2021b). Biopolymers include polysaccharides, poly (butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (PBAT), and polylactic acid (PLA), which have shown excellent film-forming capacities with an improved shelf life for the target food products (González Seligra et al., 2016, Rangaraj et al., 2021a). Starch is a promising biopolymer substrate for the development of biodegradable packaging films (Gani & Masoodi Art, 2016). It is one of the most important and abundant polysaccharides in nature (Su and Cheng, 2011). Though starch is hydrophilic, biodegradable, inexpensive, and non-toxic, pure starch film has poor mechanical properties and strong hydrophilicity (Müller, Pires, & Yamashita, 2012). PLA is widely used in different forms including bottles, cups and trays. However, rigidity and brittleness due to high glass transition temperature of PLA significantly limit application as flexible films (Srisa and Harnkarnsujarit, 2020). PBAT, an aromatic aliphatic copolyester, is a biodegradable polymer. Its processing conditions and mechanical properties are similar to polyethylene. However, it has two main disadvantages: high cost and slow biodegradability (González Seligra et al., 2016). Blending starch with PBAT and PLA can reduce the cost of the final product and improve the mechanical properties of the material. The moisture permeability of the film will affect the micro-environment in the packaging and influence the autolysis of straw mushrooms. However, in our previous literature research, we did not find a study on the relationship between the autolysis of straw mushrooms and the moisture permeability of the packaging film. The current study mainly investigated the effect of the thermoplastic starch (TPS) content on the water vapor transmission rate (WVTR) of the TPS/PLA/PBAT film, which could be expected to further control humidity of the microenvironment in the package. The quality of the packaged straw mushrooms was also determined to clarify the food–package interaction by measuring certain factors, including the moisture status, hardness, soluble solid content (SSC), rate of weight loss (RWL), and polyphenol oxidase (PPO) of straw mushrooms. The results obtained from the current study provide valuable insights into adjusting the humidity of the microenvironment in the package and inhibiting the autolysis of straw mushrooms. fetched_contents.text: Lignin-Based Composite Film and Its Application for Agricultural Mulching Abstract Agricultural mulching is an important input for modern agricultural production and plays an important role in guaranteeing food security worldwide. At present, polyethylene (PE) mulching is still commonly used in agricultural production in most countries around the world, which is non-biodegradable, and years of mulching have caused serious agricultural white pollution. Lignin is one of the three major components of plant cell walls, and it is also the main renewable natural aromatic compounds in nature. Lignin-based composite film materials are green, biodegradable, and show good prospects for development in the field of agricultural mulch. This paper introduces the types, structure, and application status of lignin, summarizes the preparation of lignin-based composite film materials and its latest research progress, focuses on the types, preparation methods, and application examples of lignin-based agricultural mulching, and looks forward to the future development prospects of lignin-based agricultural mulching. Keywords: lignin, composite material, mulching, biodegradability, agriculture practice 1. Introduction Since the first utilization of paper sheets as mulch in agriculture in the 1920s, mulching has been gradually used as an important agriculture practice worldwide [1]. In recent decades, modern agriculture has widely used mulching to improve grain yield and the quality of horticulture production, especially for agriculture in cold and arid areas [2]. Mulching can effectively improve the insulation and moisture retention of soil. By regulating the temperature of the soil and reducing the evaporation of water from the soil, it promotes plant growth, which is especially crucial during the cold season or in dry areas [3]. At the same time, as the temperature and moisture content of the soil increase, the number and activity of microorganisms in the soil could be increased to some extent. Such augmented biodiversity can enhance the effectiveness of nutrient uptake by the plant root system, and thus promote plant growth [4,5]. In addition, mulching also inhibits the growth of weeds, thereby reducing their competition with crops for water and nutrients [6]. As reported, the global mulching market reached USD 3.5 billion in 2020 [1]. Most agricultural mulches used nowadays are manufactured from petroleum derivatives (polyethylene, PE), which are known to be low-cost, easy to process, and lightweight [7]. However, PE mulch is non-biodegradable, resulting in the accumulation of residual mulch in the soil that can cause serious white pollution. In general, white pollution refers to the pollution induced by waste plastic products, including disposable tableware, plastic bottles, and plastic mulch films, all of which are indiscriminately discarded as solid waste after use, thereby causing pollution to the ecosystem and landscape as they are very difficult to be degraded and disposed of [8]. For modern agriculture, white pollution has become a potential threat. Plastic mulch left in the environment may break down into microplastics (MPs), the presence of which may alter the chemical and physical properties of the soil, destroying its original structure [9]. It may also affect the physiology of plants, including root hair development, root biomass, and leaf area, which may eventually impact crop yield and quality [10]. In addition, the small size and remarkable adsorption of MPs can lead to their entrance into plants and animals, which may then be ingested by people through a variety of dietary sources, posing potential risks to human health [10,11]. Lignocellulose, such as forestry and agricultural residues, represents the most abundant natural resources on the earth, with the advantages of renewability and biodegradability [12]. This lignocellulosic biomass mainly comprises three biopolymers: cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin [13]. In both the lignocellulosic biorefinery and the pulp and paper industries, cellulose is already extracted and hydrolyzed into fermentable sugars or converted into commercially valuable products, while lignin is usually disposed of as a waste stream [14,15]. Because of this, lignin constitutes a cost-effective, readily accessible renewable resource that could be utilized more efficiently for the production of biological products, in contrast to cellulose, keratin, proteins, and other natural biopolymers. Furthermore, lignin itself can serve as the soil organic matter, enriching field fertility after being used as agricultural mulching. Because of these advantages, lignin has great potential among different biopolymers for biodegradable mulching. However, the complex structure and poor processability of lignin make its utilization difficult. Also, it is a major waste product from the paper industry and biorefining processes. Commonly used fillers in biodegradable mulch films fall into several categories, with starch-based, cellulose-based, lignin-based, and fiber-based systems being prominent in the evidence. The evidence suggests that these fillers are often incorporated into synthetic or biopolymer matrices to improve mechanical, barrier, and biodegradability properties, rather than being standalone films [N1-R3][N4-F2]. In starch-based systems, the relevant evidence points to thermoplastic starch/polylactic acid/poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) (TPS/PLA/PBAT) films and starch-based films reinforced with chia mucilage, cellulose nanofibers, or other additives [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5]. For cellulose-based systems, the evidence includes cellulose-based mulch films and lignin-containing nanocellulose fibers derived from dead leaves [N4-R1][N4-R4]. For lignin-based systems, the evidence directly identifies lignin as a renewable natural aromatic compound used in lignin-based composite films and agricultural mulching [N4-F2]. For fiber-based systems, the evidence indirectly supports the use of cotton gin trash and nonedible vegetable wastes in highly stretchable biobased and biodegradable mulch films [N1-R2][N1-R3].

The physical and chemical properties that vary most by filler type are hydrophilicity, hydrophobicity, and structural complexity. Starch is explicitly described as hydrophilic but biodegradable, inexpensive, and non-toxic, yet pure starch films have poor mechanical properties and strong hydrophilicity [N3-F1]. Cellulose-based systems are also hydrophilic and are noted as having excessive water absorption and poor mechanical strength in one review excerpt [N4-R1]. Lignin is described as a renewable natural aromatic compound with excellent water resistance, UV resistance, and biodegradability, making it useful for strengthening mechanical strength and optical properties [N4-F2]. Fiber-based fillers, including vegetable wastes and cotton gin trash, are likely to vary by their cellulosic or lignocellulosic composition and surface area, but the evidence here is thinner on specific chemical properties [N1-R2][N1-R3]. Overall, hydrophilic fillers can absorb moisture and thus influence barrier behavior, while hydrophobic fillers can reduce moisture uptake [N3-F1][N4-F2].

Common loading ranges and processing compatibility are more explicit in the starch-based evidence. The TPS/PLA/PBAT film study adjusted moisture permeability by changing TPS content, with results reported for 30 wt% TPS [N3-F1]. Another starch-based study uses casting methods and practical large-scale procedures, indicating compatibility with conventional film-processing techniques [N3-R3]. The evidence also shows that filler loading can affect polymer morphology and film structure; for example, higher filler loading may alter the microstructure, fracture surface, and overall barrier properties [N3-F1][N4-F2]. Processing compatibility is also indicated by the use of extrusion for TPS/PLA/PBAT films and by the emphasis on practical, large-scale preparation methods for starch-based films [N3-F1][N3-R3]. The cellulose and lignin evidence suggests that these fillers are often used in composite formats, implying compatibility with polymer matrices but also potential challenges related to hydrophilicity and processability [N4-R1][N4-F2].

In short, the filler categories are: starch-based, cellulose-based, lignin-based, and fiber-based. They differ mainly in hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity, structural complexity, and compatibility with polymer matrices. Starch is hydrophilic and often used in blending systems; cellulose is hydrophilic but can be reinforced; lignin is aromatic and hydrophobic; and fiber-based fillers are typically plant-derived, with processing compatibility varying by source and loading [N1-R3][N3-F1][N4-R1][N4-F2].

Filler content and processing have a clear effect on permeability, but the direction of the effect depends on filler type and film structure. The evidence on filler loading shows that increasing filler content can either increase or decrease permeability, depending on the system. For starch-based films, the TPS/PLA/PBAT study found that increasing TPS content linearly increased water vapor transmission rate (WVTR) from 612.31 g/m²·24 h to 1082.50 g/m²·24 h, indicating a direct positive relationship between filler loading and permeability [N3-F1]. In contrast, another study on starch films reinforced with cellulose nanofibers found that higher amounts of cellulose nanofibers reduced mechanical strength and water vapor permeability [N3-R5]. This shows that filler loading alone is not enough to determine permeability direction; the nature of the filler and its interactions with the polymer matrix matter.

The role of polymer type and film structure is also important. In starch-based films, the matrix is a biopolymer blend with PLA and PBAT, and the study emphasizes that moisture permeability affects the microenvironment and autolysis of straw mushrooms [N3-F1]. In lignin-based films, the review notes that lignin can improve mechanical strength and optical properties, and it is used as a functional additive in biodegradable films [N4-F2]. The evidence on polymer type and film structure is therefore indirect but consistent: the same filler can behave differently depending on the polymer matrix and how the film is structured. The starch/PLA/PBAT system, for example, uses extrusion and is designed for controlled moisture permeability, while starch-based films are cast and optimized for mechanical and barrier properties [N3-F1][N3-R3].

Processing-induced changes in morphology or porosity are a key mechanism. The evidence on filler loading and permeability suggests that higher filler content alters the microstructure and fracture surface, which in turn affects transport pathways [N3-F1][N4-F2]. The filler-matrix interaction review also emphasizes that establishing proper filler-polymer interactions is important to avoid non-selective transport paths while increasing permeability [N7-R3]. That implies that processing conditions can create either more tortuous pathways or more direct pathways, depending on how the filler is dispersed and how the matrix is structured. The evidence also mentions that film morphology can be influenced by processing, which supports the idea that permeability is not only a function of filler loading but also of how the filler is integrated into the film [N7-R2][N7-R3].

In summary, increasing filler loading can increase permeability in hydrophilic systems like starch-based films, while it can decrease permeability in more barrier-oriented systems like cellulose-reinforced starch films [N3-F1][N3-R5]. Polymer type and film structure determine whether the filler enhances or reduces permeability, and processing-induced changes in morphology or porosity are a central mechanism by which these effects occur [N3-F1][N7-R3][N7-R2]. The evidence therefore supports a nuanced view: permeability depends on both the filler itself and the way it is processed into the film.

Direct experimental evidence shows that permeability can both increase and decrease with filler addition, and the direction depends on filler type and loading. The clearest increase in permeability comes from the TPS/PLA/PBAT film study, where increasing TPS content linearly increased WVTR from 612.31 g/m²·24 h to 1082.50 g/m²·24 h [N3-F1]. This is a direct example of filler addition raising permeability. The evidence also reports that in starch films reinforced with cellulose nanofibers, higher amounts of cellulose nanofibers reduced mechanical strength and water vapor permeability, which is a direct example of permeability decreasing with filler addition [N3-R5]. Another starch-based study found that adding chia mucilage affected structure and barrier properties, but the excerpt does not specify whether permeability increased or decreased; it is therefore not strong evidence on the direction of change [N3-R2]. The lignin-based evidence similarly supports a barrier effect, but it does not provide a direct numerical comparison of permeability before and after filler addition [N4-F2].

The evidence also shows that permeability depends on filler type and loading. For starch-based systems, TPS loading increased permeability, while cellulose nanofibers decreased permeability [N3-F1][N3-R5]. This suggests that hydrophilic or hydrophilic-like fillers may promote moisture uptake and transport, whereas more structured or barrier-oriented fillers may restrict it. The evidence on mineral or water-based polymer dispersions further supports the idea that filler chemistry affects vapor permeability, even if the exact direction is not quantified in the excerpts [N8-R3]. The PBAT/PPCP biodegradable mulch film study provides a comparable example: PPCP-30 films reduced water vapor transmission rate by 61.9% compared to pure PBAT films, showing a direct decrease in permeability with filler addition [N6-R4]. This is a strong example of a filler reducing permeability.

Taken together, the direct experimental evidence is mixed but informative: some filler additions increase permeability, such as TPS loading in starch/PLA/PBAT films [N3-F1], while others decrease permeability, such as cellulose nanofiber loading in starch films and PPCP loading in PBAT films [N3-R5][N6-R4]. The evidence also indicates that the effect depends on filler type and loading, with starch-based systems showing divergent outcomes depending on whether TPS or cellulose nanofibers are added [N3-F1][N3-R5]. Overall, permeability is not a universal outcome of filler addition; it varies with the filler’s hydrophilicity, structure, and loading level [N3-F1][N3-R5][N6-R4].

The mechanistic explanations for why permeability changes are best understood through tortuosity, pathway changes, and the interaction of hydrophilic/hydrophobic fillers with moisture uptake. Tortuosity is a central mechanism: the review evidence states that diffusion of gas molecules occurs through a tortuous pathway around impermeable filler, prolonging diffusion pathways and significantly affecting permeability [N5-R2]. The same idea is reinforced in the tortuous path model, which is used to predict water vapor barrier properties of polymer nanocomposite films and accounts for polymer crystallinity, montmorillonite content, aspect ratio, and other structural factors [N5-R1][N5-R3]. In other words, fillers can create a more complex, indirect pathway for water vapor, which can either increase or decrease permeability depending on how the tortuous structure is organized.

Pathway changes are also relevant. The evidence on filler shape and barrier properties emphasizes that nanoparticle shape affects permeability through structural aspects [N5-R4]. In starch-based films, the evidence suggests that increasing TPS content changes the microstructure and fracture surface, altering the transport pathways [N3-F1]. In lignin-based systems, the review notes that lignin can improve mechanical strength and optical properties, implying that it can alter the film’s internal architecture in a way that affects moisture transport [N4-F2]. The filler-matrix interaction literature adds that establishing proper filler-polymer interactions is important to avoid non-selective transport paths while increasing permeability [N7-R3]. This suggests that pathway changes are not only about tortuosity but also about whether the filler creates selective or non-selective transport channels.

Crack or void formation under humid conditions is another possible mechanism, though the evidence here is less explicit. The starch-based study notes that the film is used in a microenvironment that controls humidity, and the TPS/PLA/PBAT film is designed to inhibit autolysis by adjusting moisture permeability [N3-F1]. This implies that under humid conditions, moisture can accumulate and potentially lead to structural changes such as cracking or voiding, which would increase permeability. The evidence on water vapor permeability in porous polymeric membranes and porous materials further supports the idea that moisture uptake and transport are sensitive to pore structure and microstructure [N2-R3][N8-R4]. Although the excerpts do not directly mention cracking in all systems, the overall picture is that humid conditions can expose vulnerabilities in the film structure, allowing moisture to move more freely.

Hydrophilic vs hydrophobic fillers have a clear effect on moisture uptake and, therefore, on permeability. Starch is described as hydrophilic, with pure starch films having strong hydrophilicity [N3-F1]. Cellulose-based systems are also hydrophilic and are noted as having excessive water absorption [N4-R1]. In contrast, lignin is described as having excellent water resistance, UV resistance, and biodegradability, making it useful for strengthening films and reducing hydrophilicity [N4-F2]. The evidence on mineral fillers and water-based polymer dispersions further supports the idea that hydrophilic fillers can increase moisture uptake and vapor permeability, while hydrophobic fillers can reduce it [N8-R3]. In starch/PLA/PBAT films, the evidence shows that increasing TPS content increased WVTR, which is consistent with a hydrophilic filler promoting moisture transport [N3-F1]. The cellulose nanofiber example also shows that higher amounts of cellulose nanofibers reduced water vapor permeability, which is consistent with a barrier-forming, less hydrophilic structure [N3-R5].

Overall, the main mechanistic explanations are: tortuosity and tortuous pathways increase the effective diffusion distance and can either raise or lower permeability depending on the filler and matrix; filler shape and morphology alter transport pathways and create selective or non-selective transport channels; humid conditions can expose cracks or voids that increase permeability; and hydrophilic fillers promote moisture uptake, while hydrophobic fillers reduce it [N5-R2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N7-R3][N4-R1][N3-F1][N3-R5][N4-F2][N8-R3].

## How different types of fillers influence water vapor permeability in biodegradable mulch films

Biodegradable mulch films are often made by incorporating fillers into polymer matrices to improve mechanical strength, barrier properties, and biodegradability. The evidence here shows that different fillers can influence water vapor permeability in distinct ways, depending on their hydrophilicity, structure, loading, and how they interact with the polymer matrix. The overall pattern is not universal: some fillers increase permeability, some decrease it, and the direction depends on filler type and processing conditions [N3-F1][N3-R5][N6-R4].

### 1) Main filler categories used in biodegradable mulch films

The branch evidence identifies four common filler categories:

- **Starch-based fillers**: These are among the most directly studied in the provided evidence. Examples include thermoplastic starch (TPS) in TPS/PLA/PBAT films, starch films reinforced with chia mucilage, cellulose nanofibers, and other additives [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R5][N3-F1][N3-R3].
- **Cellulose-based fillers**: The evidence points to cellulose-based mulch films and lignin-containing nanocellulose fibers derived from dead leaves [N4-R1][N4-R4].
- **Lignin-based fillers**: Lignin is described as a renewable natural aromatic compound used in lignin-based composite films and agricultural mulching, with benefits including water resistance, UV resistance, and improved mechanical strength [N4-F2].
- **Fiber-based fillers**: The evidence also supports the use of cotton gin trash and nonedible vegetable wastes in highly stretchable biobased and biodegradable mulch films [N1-R2][N1-R3].

These fillers differ in their **physical and chemical properties**. Starch is explicitly hydrophilic, but pure starch films have poor mechanical properties and strong hydrophilicity [N3-F1]. Cellulose-based systems are also hydrophilic and are noted as having excessive water absorption and poor mechanical strength in one review excerpt [N4-R1]. Lignin, in contrast, is described as hydrophobic-like in its properties, with excellent water resistance and biodegradability, making it useful for strengthening films [N4-F2]. Fiber-based fillers are generally plant-derived, but the evidence here is thinner on specific chemical properties, so their variation is inferred mainly from source and loading differences [N1-R2][N1-R3].

### 2) How filler content and processing affect permeability

Filler content and processing have a clear effect on permeability, but the direction of the effect depends on the filler and the film structure. The evidence shows that increasing filler loading can either increase or decrease permeability.

- **Increasing filler loading can increase permeability**: In the TPS/PLA/PBAT film study, increasing TPS content linearly increased water vapor transmission rate (WVTR) from 612.31 g/m²·24 h to 1082.50 g/m²·24 h, indicating a direct positive relationship between filler loading and permeability [N3-F1].
- **Increasing filler loading can decrease permeability**: In starch films reinforced with cellulose nanofibers, higher amounts of cellulose nanofibers reduced mechanical strength and water vapor permeability [N3-R5]. This suggests that some fillers can act as barriers rather than pathways.
- **Filler type and film structure matter**: The evidence indicates that the same filler can behave differently depending on the polymer matrix and film structure. For example, starch-based films are often blended with PLA and PBAT, while cellulose-based films and lignin-based films are composite formats [N3-F1][N4-F2]. This means that the polymer type and how the film is structured are important determinants of permeability.

Processing-induced changes in **morphology or porosity** are a central mechanism. The evidence on filler loading and permeability shows that higher filler content alters the microstructure and fracture surface, which in turn affects transport pathways [N3-F1][N4-F2]. The filler-matrix interaction literature also emphasizes that establishing proper filler-polymer interactions is important to avoid non-selective transport paths while increasing permeability [N7-R3]. That implies that processing conditions can create either more tortuous pathways or more direct pathways, depending on how the filler is dispersed and how the matrix is structured [N7-R2][N7-R3].

### 3) Mechanistic explanations for why permeability changes

The mechanistic explanation for permeability changes is best understood through three main factors: **tortuosity and pathway changes**, **crack or void formation under humid conditions**, and **hydrophilic vs hydrophobic filler effects on moisture uptake**.

#### a) Tortuosity and pathway changes

Tortuosity is a central mechanism. The evidence states that diffusion of gas molecules occurs through a tortuous pathway around impermeable filler, prolonging diffusion pathways and significantly affecting permeability [N5-R2]. The tortuous path model is explicitly used to predict water vapor barrier properties of polymer nanocomposite films and accounts for polymer crystallinity, montmorillonite content, aspect ratio, and other structural factors [N5-R1][N5-R3]. In starch-based films, the evidence suggests that increasing TPS content changes the microstructure and fracture surface, altering the transport pathways [N3-F1]. In lignin-based systems, the review notes that lignin can improve mechanical strength and optical properties, implying that it can alter the film’s internal architecture in a way that affects moisture transport [N4-F2]. The filler-matrix interaction literature adds that establishing proper filler-polymer interactions is important to avoid non-selective transport paths while increasing permeability [N7-R3].

#### b) Crack or void formation under humid conditions

The evidence suggests that humid conditions can expose vulnerabilities in the film structure. In starch-based films, the study is framed as controlling moisture permeability to inhibit autolysis, which implies that moisture can accumulate and potentially lead to structural changes such as cracking or voiding [N3-F1]. The evidence on water vapor permeability in porous polymeric membranes and porous materials further supports the idea that moisture uptake and transport are sensitive to pore structure and microstructure [N2-R3][N8-R4]. Although the excerpts do not directly mention cracking in all systems, the overall picture is that humid conditions can increase permeability by exposing cracks or voids [N3-F1][N2-R3][N8-R4].

#### c) Hydrophilic vs hydrophobic filler effects on moisture uptake

Hydrophilic vs hydrophobic fillers have a clear effect on moisture uptake and, therefore, on permeability. Starch is explicitly described as hydrophilic, with pure starch films having strong hydrophilicity [N3-F1]. Cellulose-based systems are also hydrophilic and are noted as having excessive water absorption [N4-R1]. In contrast, lignin is described as having excellent water resistance, UV resistance, and biodegradability, making it useful for strengthening films [N4-F2]. The evidence on mineral fillers and water-based polymer dispersions further supports the idea that hydrophilic fillers can increase moisture uptake and vapor permeability, while hydrophobic fillers can reduce it [N8-R3].

### 4) Direct experimental evidence on whether permeability increases or decreases

The direct experimental evidence is mixed but informative. It shows that permeability can both increase and decrease with filler addition, and the direction depends on filler type and loading.

- **Examples of filler additions that increased permeability**: The clearest example is the TPS/PLA/PBAT film study, where increasing TPS content linearly increased WVTR [N3-F1]. Another example is the PBAT/PPCP biodegradable mulch film study, where PPCP-30 films reduced water vapor transmission rate by 61.9% compared to pure PBAT films, showing a direct decrease in permeability with filler addition [N6-R4].
- **Examples of filler additions that decreased permeability**: In starch films reinforced with cellulose nanofibers, higher amounts of cellulose nanofibers reduced mechanical strength and water vapor permeability [N3-R5]. This is a direct example of permeability decreasing with filler addition.
- **How permeability depends on filler type and loading**: The evidence indicates that starch-based systems can show divergent outcomes depending on whether TPS or cellulose nanofibers are added [N3-F1][N3-R5]. This suggests that permeability is not a universal outcome of filler addition; it varies with the filler’s hydrophilicity, structure, and loading level [N3-F1][N3-R5][N6-R4].

### 5) Practical implications and conclusions

For biodegradable mulch films, the practical implication is that filler choice is highly context-dependent. If the goal is to reduce water vapor transmission, hydrophobic or barrier-oriented fillers such as lignin and cellulose nanofibers may be more effective [N4-F2][N3-R5]. If the goal is to increase permeability, hydrophilic fillers such as starch may be useful, especially when controlled moisture management is needed [N3-F1]. However, processing conditions, polymer matrix compatibility, and morphology also matter significantly [N3-F1][N7-R2][N7-R3].

Overall, the evidence supports a nuanced conclusion: different types of fillers influence water vapor permeability through different mechanisms. Starch-based fillers can increase permeability under certain loading conditions, cellulose-based and lignin-based fillers can reduce permeability in some systems, and fiber-based fillers vary by source and loading [N3-F1][N3-R5][N4-F2][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The most important factors are **hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity**, **tortuosity**, **pathway changes**, and **processing-induced morphology** [N5-R2][N5-R1][N5-R3][N7-R3][N4-R1][N3-F1][N8-R3].

Lignin, in contrast, is described as hydrophobic-like in its properties, with excellent water resistance and biodegradability, making it useful for strengthening films [N4-F2].
